text: These are the kings of the land whom the Israelites defeated, taking possession of their territory east of the Jordan, from the Arnon Gorge to Mount Hermon, including all the eastern Arabah:

Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon. His rule extended from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Gorge—from the middle of the gorge—over half of Gilead as far as the Jabbok River, the border of the Ammonites,
and over the Arabah as far as the Sea of Kinnereth on the east, and to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, on the east toward Beth Jeshimoth, and southward below the slopes of Pisgah.
Next was the territory of Og king of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, who reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei.

versions.text: And the territory of Og king of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, who reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei.
versions.explanation: Opening a sentence with "And the territory of" reads awkwardly aloud, since the noun phrase has no clear verb. A short lead-in keeps the list flowing naturally for oral reading without adding content.

text: He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah, and all of Bashan up to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and over half of Gilead as far as the territory of Sihon king of Heshbon.
Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the Israelites defeated them, and Moses gave their land as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

versions.text: Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the Israelites defeated them, and Moses, the servant of the LORD, gave their land as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
versions.explanation: The full title is repeated in Hebrew, but in English the double "Moses, the servant of the LORD" within one breath group makes the sentence heavy for reading aloud; the second occurrence can be shortened without loss of meaning. (If the repetition is wanted for emphasis, the verse may be left as is.)

text: These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites defeated west of the Jordan, from Baal Gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir. Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession, according to their allotted portions:
the hill country, the western foothills, the Arabah, the mountain slopes, the wilderness, and the Negev—the lands of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
The king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, near Bethel, one;
the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;
the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;
the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;
the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;
the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;
the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;
the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;
the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;
the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;
the king of Shimron Meron, one; the king of Akshaph, one;
the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;
the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;
the king of Dor in Naphath Dor, one; the king of Goyim in Gilgal, one;
the king of Tirzah, one. Thirty-one kings in all.
